glass-amorphous-001.question: Which statement about the atomic arrangement of an oxide glass such as soda-lime glass is correct?
choices: Nearest-neighbor coordination and bond lengths, as in SiO₄ tetrahedra, are nearly uniform (short-range order), but there is no long-range periodicity
The atoms are arranged completely at random, like a gas, and both the coordination number and the bond lengths vary from atom to atom
It has the same periodic arrangement as a crystal, but its grains are only a few nm across, so no peaks appear in X-ray diffraction
glass-amorphous-001.explanation: Even in an oxide glass, the SiO₄ unit, in which four oxygens are tetrahedrally coordinated around Si, is almost the same as in the crystal, and the Si-O distance is uniform. However, the Si-O-Si angles and the way tetrahedra link vary, so regularity is lost beyond about 1 nm and there is no long-range periodicity. Zachariasen described this as a continuous random network. In X-ray diffraction a broad halo appears instead of sharp peaks, and the nearest-neighbor distance and coordination number can be obtained from the radial distribution function. The statement that atoms are completely disordered overlooks short-range order. The crystallite hypothesis, which treats glass as an aggregate of tiny crystals, is not the main view, because the crystal size estimated from the halo width is no larger than a unit cell, and the small-angle scattering that grain boundaries would produce is not observed (Warren).

glass-amorphous-002.question: Which set correctly lists network-forming oxides, which form glass on their own and build the network skeleton of oxide glasses?
choices: Na₂O, K₂O, CaO
Al₂O₃, MgO, ZnO
SiO₂, B₂O₃, P₂O₅
glass-amorphous-002.explanation: In SiO₂, B₂O₃, P₂O₅ and GeO₂, the cations form polyhedra with three- or fourfold oxygen coordination that link by sharing their corner oxygens, so each forms a glass network on its own. Zachariasen named conditions such as a small cation coordination number and polyhedra sharing only corners, not edges or faces, as favoring glass formation. Na₂O, K₂O and CaO are network modifiers: they break the network and occupy its interstices, and they do not form glass by themselves. Al₂O₃ and ZnO are called intermediate oxides; they hardly form glass alone, but when their charge is compensated by alkalis and the like they join the network, for example as AlO₄ tetrahedra. MgO usually acts as a modifier.

glass-amorphous-003.question: How do the structure and properties of SiO₂ glass change when Na₂O is added?
choices: Na⁺ takes the place of Si⁴⁺ at the center of SiO₄ tetrahedra and strengthens the network, so the viscosity and softening temperature rise
Si-O-Si bridges break into non-bridging oxygens and the network weakens, so the viscosity and the glass transition temperature fall and thermal expansion increases
Na₂O does not affect the network, so the viscosity is unchanged and only the chemical durability improves
glass-amorphous-003.explanation: Each Na₂O added breaks one Si-O-Si bridging oxygen and creates two non-bridging oxygens bonded to only one Si, while the Na⁺ ions occupy interstices in the network and balance the charge. The weakened connectivity lowers the viscosity and the glass transition temperature, so shaping that requires high temperatures of about 2000 °C for silica glass becomes possible at much lower temperatures. In exchange, the linear expansion coefficient increases, and because Na⁺ readily exchanges with hydrogen ions in water, chemical durability falls. CaO is added in soda-lime glass to restore this durability. Na⁺ has a large ionic radius and small charge, so it does not enter the centers of tetrahedra.

glass-amorphous-004.question: In a sodium silicate glass of 30 mol% Na₂O-70 mol% SiO₂, assuming each Na₂O creates two non-bridging oxygens, which is closest to the number of non-bridging oxygens per SiO₄ tetrahedron (NBO/T)?
choices: About 0.43
About 0.60
About 0.86
glass-amorphous-004.explanation: One mole of Na₂O creates two moles of non-bridging oxygens, so NBO/T = 2×30/70 ≈ 0.86. On average, 0.86 corner oxygens per tetrahedron are not linked to a neighboring tetrahedron, lowering the degree of network connectivity. About 0.43 is the value obtained by counting one non-bridging oxygen per Na₂O, and about 0.60 is the value obtained by dividing by the total 100 mol instead of the number of tetrahedra (the amount of SiO₂). NBO/T = 0 means a fully three-dimensional network as in silica glass, 2 means SiO₄ linked in chains or rings, and 4 means isolated tetrahedra. NBO/T is often used as a guide to viscosity and other properties when comparing the compositions of glasses and slags.

glass-amorphous-005.question: The viscosity η (Pa·s) of a soda-lime glass is described by the VFT equation log₁₀η = A + B/(T − T₀) with A = −2.5, B = 4300 K and T₀ = 520 K. Which is closest to the temperature at which the viscosity reaches 10¹² Pa·s (a guide to the annealing point, close to the glass transition temperature)?
choices: About 817 K
About 878 K
About 297 K
glass-amorphous-005.explanation: Setting log₁₀η = 12 gives T − T₀ = B/(12 − A) = 4300/14.5 ≈ 297 K, so T ≈ 520 + 297 = 817 K (about 543 °C). The VFT equation has the viscosity rise steeply, as if diverging, on approaching T₀, and it can express a stronger temperature dependence than the Arrhenius form. About 878 K is the value obtained by ignoring A and taking B/12, and about 297 K is the value obtained by forgetting to add T₀. In glass processing, articles are formed at the working point, where the viscosity is about 10³ Pa·s, held near the annealing point of about 10¹² Pa·s, and then cooled slowly to below the strain point (about 3×10¹³ Pa·s) to remove residual stress. Knowing how viscosity changes with temperature is the basis for setting forming and annealing conditions.

glass-amorphous-006.question: Which correctly describes how sheet glass is strengthened by air quenching (thermal tempering)?
choices: Quenching leaves tension at the surface and compression in the interior, and the internal compression stops cracks from growing so the glass resists breaking
Quenching makes the surfaces solidify first, and the interior, cooling and shrinking later, pulls them into compression and goes into tension itself
Quenching crystallizes only the surface, forming a hard crystalline layer that prevents scratches and so resists breaking
glass-amorphous-006.explanation: When air is blown on both faces of a glass sheet heated to about 650 °C, the surfaces cool and solidify first. The interior is still soft at this stage, so the shrinkage of the surfaces is absorbed by flow in the interior. When the interior later cools and tries to shrink, it pulls in the already rigid surfaces, so at room temperature compressive stress in the surfaces and tensile stress inside remain in balance. Glass fracture starts in tension from surface flaws, so the glass does not break until the applied tension exceeds the surface compression, and its strength becomes about 3–5 times that of annealed glass. However, when it breaks, the strain energy stored inside shatters the whole sheet into small granules, and it cannot be cut after tempering. The statement that tension remains at the surface has it backward, and no crystallization takes place.

glass-amorphous-007.question: In thermally tempered glass of thickness t = 10 mm, let y be the distance from the mid-plane; the stress follows the parabolic distribution σ(y) = σc(1 − 12y²/t²) (tension positive, σc is the tensile stress at the mid-plane). If the surface compressive stress is 120 MPa, which correctly pairs the mid-plane tensile stress σc with the depth from the surface to the end of the compressive layer?
choices: About 120 MPa, about 2.1 mm
About 60 MPa, about 2.1 mm
About 60 MPa, about 2.9 mm
glass-amorphous-007.explanation: At the surface, y = t/2, σ = σc(1 − 3) = −2σc, so 2σc = 120 MPa gives σc = 60 MPa. The stress is zero where 12y²/t² = 1, that is, at y = t/√12 ≈ 2.89 mm, so the depth from the surface is 5.0 − 2.89 ≈ 2.1 mm (about 21% of the thickness). This distribution satisfies force balance: summed through the thickness, the stress is zero. About 2.9 mm takes the distance measured from the mid-plane as the depth from the surface. A pairing with the mid-plane tension equal to the 120 MPa surface compression does not satisfy force balance. A surface compression about twice the mid-plane tension and a compressive layer about one fifth of the thickness are the usual guidelines for thermal tempering.

glass-amorphous-008.question: Which correctly describes chemical strengthening (strengthening by ion exchange), used for smartphone cover glass and similar products?
choices: Below the strain point, Na⁺ in the surface layer is exchanged for larger K⁺, creating compressive stress in the surface layer
Na⁺ in the surface layer is exchanged for the smaller Li⁺, which shrinks the volume of the surface layer and so creates compressive stress
Carrying out the ion exchange above the softening point makes it proceed faster and so gives a larger compressive stress to a greater depth
glass-amorphous-008.explanation: In chemical strengthening, a glass containing Na⁺ is immersed in molten KNO₃ at about 400 °C. When Na⁺ in the surface layer is replaced by larger K⁺, the larger ions are in effect squeezed into sites sized for Na⁺; the surface layer tries to expand but is constrained by the interior, so a large compressive stress of several hundred MPa or more develops in it. This temperature is below the strain point, where the network hardly flows, so the stress remains without relaxing. Above the softening point, the stress would relax by viscous flow. If the surface layer tried to shrink through exchange for smaller Li⁺, tensile stress would arise in it instead. Thermal tempering is difficult for thin sheets, in which it is hard to set up a temperature difference, whereas chemical strengthening can be used even on sheets 1 mm thick or less.

glass-amorphous-009.question: Which combination is the empirically known set of conditions (Inoue's empirical rules) for alloys that readily form bulk metallic glasses, which become glass even at thicknesses of several mm or more?
choices: The alloy consists of only two elements, close in composition to a high-melting pure metal, with a high liquidus temperature
Three or more elements of nearly equal atomic radius are combined so that the heat of mixing between them is positive
It has three or more elements, with main-element atomic radii differing by about 12% or more and a negative heat of mixing
glass-amorphous-009.explanation: Inoue's empirical rules are three: multiple components, an atomic radius difference of about 12% or more among the main elements, and a negative heat of mixing. When atoms of different sizes mix while attracting one another, the liquid takes a densely packed, disordered arrangement, and atomic diffusion and rearrangement slow down. In addition, forming a crystal from a liquid containing many elements requires extensive rearrangement of atoms, so crystal nucleation and growth become difficult. A lower liquidus temperature at compositions near a deep eutectic also helps. Combinations with equal atomic radii and positive heat of mixing tend to form solid solutions or phase-separate, and compositions close to a pure metal hardly become glass even with quenching at about 10⁶ K/s.

glass-amorphous-010.question: By Turnbull's guideline, the larger the reduced glass transition temperature Trg = Tg/Tl (Tg is the glass transition temperature and Tl the liquidus temperature, both absolute temperatures), the more readily a melt becomes glass on cooling. Which of the following alloys forms glass most readily by this guideline?
choices: The alloy with Tg = 625 K and Tl = 940 K
The alloy with Tg = 420 K and Tl = 820 K
The alloy with Tg = 700 K and Tl = 1300 K
glass-amorphous-010.explanation: Calculating Trg gives 625/940 ≈ 0.665 for the alloy with Tg = 625 K and Tl = 940 K, about 0.538 for the alloy with Tg = 700 K and Tl = 1300 K, and about 0.512 for the alloy with Tg = 420 K and Tl = 820 K. The narrower the temperature span from Tl to Tg, the more quickly the melt passes through the supercooled-liquid range in which crystals can nucleate and grow, and the liquid in that range is also more viscous, so glass forms more easily. Turnbull estimated that crystallization is strongly suppressed once Trg reaches about 2/3 or more. The alloy with the highest Tg or the lowest Tl is not necessarily the one chosen; what matters is their ratio. This is an empirical guideline with exceptions.

glass-amorphous-011.question: Sheet-shaped metallic glass is made by casting into a copper mold. Assume that the cooling rate at the center of the sheet is inversely proportional to the square of the thickness d, and that it is 1.0×10³ K/s for a thickness of 1.0 mm. Which is closest to the largest thickness at which an alloy with a critical cooling rate of 10 K/s can be made into glass?
choices: About 100 mm
About 0.10 mm
About 10 mm
glass-amorphous-011.explanation: The cooling rate can be written R = 1.0×10³×(1.0/d)² K/s (d in mm), so the thickness at which R = 10 K/s is d = 1.0×√(1.0×10³/10) = 10 mm. The time for heat to escape to the mold is proportional to the square of the distance heat must travel, so the cooling rate is inversely proportional to the square of the thickness. About 100 mm assumes the cooling rate is inversely proportional to the thickness itself, and about 0.10 mm inverts the ratio of cooling rates. Early metallic glasses had large critical cooling rates of about 10⁵–10⁶ K/s, so only ribbons a few tens of µm thick made by melt spinning could be obtained, but multicomponent alloys lowered the critical cooling rate and made centimeter-scale bulk metallic glasses possible.

glass-amorphous-012.question: A Zr-based bulk metallic glass has a yield strength of 1.8 GPa and a Young's modulus of 90 GPa. Which correctly pairs the elastic strain limit estimated as σy/E with its comparison to crystalline metallic materials?
choices: About 0.020%, smaller than most crystalline metallic materials
About 2.0%, larger than most crystalline metallic materials (below 1%)
About 2.0%, about the same as most crystalline metallic materials
glass-amorphous-012.explanation: σy/E = 1.8/90 = 0.020, that is, about 2.0%. For steel (yield stress 0.5 GPa, Young's modulus 200 GPa) it is about 0.25%, and even for a high-strength titanium alloy (0.9 GPa, 110 GPa) about 0.8%, so the elastic strain limit of the metallic glass is much larger. This is because metallic glasses have no dislocations and therefore high yield strength, while their Young's modulus is often about 30% lower than that of crystals of the same composition. The elastic energy stored per unit volume, σy²/(2E), is a large 18 MJ/m³ or so, which is exploited in springs, golf club faces and the like. About 0.020% is the value obtained by forgetting to convert 0.020 into a percentage.

glass-amorphous-013.question: Which statement about plastic deformation of metallic glasses at room temperature is correct?
choices: The yield strength is high, but deformation concentrates in thin shear bands, so in tension they tend to fracture with almost no elongation
With no grain boundaries they are highly ductile and elongate uniformly by several tens of percent in a room-temperature tensile test before fracturing
Dislocations glide in them just as in crystals, so they work-harden strongly, and they neck extensively before fracturing in a ductile manner
glass-amorphous-013.explanation: In metallic glasses, shear stress makes small groups of atoms move cooperatively, locally increasing free volume and softening the material. Because this softening invites further deformation, deformation concentrates in shear bands about 10 to a few tens of nm thick, and with no work hardening, a single shear band runs through the specimen in tension and it fractures with almost no elongation. In compression and bending, many shear bands form and some plastic deformation is seen. Work hardening and necking by dislocation glide are features of crystalline metals, and the absence of grain boundaries does not guarantee ductility. As a countermeasure, composites with dispersed crystalline phases that hinder shear band propagation are being studied. In the supercooled-liquid range, on the other hand, metallic glasses can deform greatly by viscous flow, which is used for precision forming.

glass-amorphous-014.question: Amorphous silicon for solar cells and thin-film transistors is made by plasma CVD from silane as a-Si:H containing about 10% hydrogen. What is the main reason?
choices: Hydrogen acts as an interstitial donor and makes the film n-type even without phosphorus doping
Hydrogen promotes crystallization of Si and turns the film into high-mobility polycrystalline silicon, improving its properties
Hydrogen terminates Si dangling bonds and so reduces defect levels in the band gap
glass-amorphous-014.explanation: Amorphous silicon without hydrogen contains as many as about 10¹⁹–10²⁰ cm⁻³ dangling bonds without a partner because of network disorder, and the levels they create near the middle of the band gap trap electrons and holes. As a result, adding dopants barely moves the Fermi level, and carriers generated by light recombine quickly. When hydrogen terminates these with Si-H bonds, the defect density falls to about 10¹⁵–10¹⁶ cm⁻³, making n-type and p-type doping with phosphorus or boron possible. Hydrogen does not act as a donor, and under ordinary deposition conditions the film stays amorphous (silane strongly diluted with hydrogen can also give microcrystalline films, but that serves a different purpose). The Staebler–Wronski effect, in which prolonged illumination increases defects, is also related to this hydrogen.

glass-amorphous-015.question: Which correctly compares the properties of hydrogenated amorphous silicon (a-Si:H) and crystalline silicon?
choices: Its disordered atomic arrangement means it absorbs almost no visible light, so it is used for transparent electrodes in place of ITO
It absorbs visible light more strongly than crystalline silicon, so films under 1 µm suffice, but its electron mobility is 2 to 3 orders lower
Its electron mobility is higher than that of crystalline silicon, so it is widely used in place of it for transistors in high-speed microprocessors
glass-amorphous-015.explanation: Crystalline silicon is an indirect-gap semiconductor that absorbs the longer wavelengths of visible light weakly, so solar cells usually use substrates 100 µm thick or more. In a-Si:H there is no long-range periodicity, so the constraint of conserving momentum in a transition is relaxed and its visible absorption coefficient is larger than that of the crystal, letting a film 1 µm thick or less absorb the light. On the other hand, carriers are trapped in band-tail states created by the disordered network, so the electron mobility is about 1–10 cm²/(V·s), 2 to 3 orders of magnitude lower than the roughly 1400 cm²/(V·s) of crystalline silicon. It is therefore unsuited to high-speed logic circuits, but taking advantage of large-area deposition at about 300 °C, it has been used for pixel TFTs in liquid crystal displays and for thin-film solar cells. With a band gap of about 1.7 eV it absorbs visible light strongly and cannot be a transparent electrode.
